claims.text: The initial cast multi-principal element alloy has a coarse-grained microstructure.
The initial cast multi-principal element alloy has limited ductility.
Severe plastic deformation followed by controlled low-temperature annealing will produce grains smaller than 50 nm.
The proposed processing route will produce a dual-phase solid-solution structure.
The proposed processing route will enhance yield strength.
Keeping the annealing temperature below the critical intermetallic-nucleation threshold will prevent brittle intermetallic formation.
Annealing above the temperature required for partial recrystallization will stabilize the nanocrystalline grains.
Severe plastic deformation generates a high density of dislocations and grain boundaries.
Dislocations and grain boundaries act as sinks for solute segregation.
The deformation-induced defect structure stabilizes the dual-phase solid solution against grain coarsening.
The deformation-induced defect structure stabilizes the dual-phase solid solution against phase separation.
Severe plastic deformation refines the grains to the nanoscale.
Thermodynamic stability of the dual-phase solid solution prevents brittle intermetallic nucleation during subsequent annealing.
Sluggish diffusion characteristic of multi-principal element alloys kinetically suppresses brittle intermetallic nucleation.
The processed material will have significantly greater hardness than the cast baseline.
The processed material will have significantly greater yield strength than the cast baseline.
The processed material will retain ductility relative to the cast form.
The microstructure becomes unstable when annealing temperature exceeds the critical limit at which the driving force for intermetallic formation overcomes the diffusion-related kinetic barrier.
Insufficient deformation strain will fail to generate the defect density needed for nanocrystalline grain refinement.
